Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-15
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 48 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen, Ravi Patel, Lena Ortiz (Redwood) — Jenna Morris, Carlos Vega, Priya Singh, Tom Reyes (Aperture)

Auto-summary (AI): Quick sync to review pilot throughput numbers from last 48 hours, align on continuous-batching profile adjustments, pick target concurrency and queue depth for 4h steady-state run, and confirm next steps for security/production readiness. Some minor audio artifacts; speaker labels approximate.

Topics:
- Recent throughput runs (24h burst + 12h smoothing)
- Continuous batching tweaks (max batch size, batch timeout)
- Concurrency targets and p95/p99 tail latency tradeoffs
- Queue depth, backpressure and retry policy
- Fallback model variants, burst capacity and on-demand scaling
- Next steps and owners

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call — can you confirm audio?
[00:06] Jenna Morris: Yep good here. Carlos, Priya?
[00:08] Carlos Vega: here, can hear you Maya.
[00:10] Priya Singh: yes.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Cool. We'll spend about forty five minutes. Ravi will walk through the tuned batching profiles and we want to decide the 4 hour steady state run parameters.
[00:21] Ravi Patel: hi all. Quick tl;dr: last 48 hour run showed nominal throughput 2.3k tok/s with continuous batching on the small seq path, but we saw p99 spikes when concurrency crossed ~180. We adjusted the batch_timeout from 12ms to 8ms which helped average latency but reduced effective batch utilization a bit.
[00:41] Tom Reyes: when you say tok/s is that per GPU or cluster?
[00:44] Ravi Patel: cluster aggregate across 4 dedicated GPUs in the pilot pool — nominally g4gn type but it's our density profile.
[00:52] Jenna Morris: Quick correction — those are A100-equivalent nodes in our dedicated pack, not g4. Some of the notes auto-transcribed hardware incorrectly earlier, so apologies if my ticket said g4.
[01:02] Maya Chen: noted, thanks. 
[01:05] Speaker 3: (unintelligible) the baseline cost numbers look fine.
[01:12] Ravi Patel: On the point of p99: the spikes were correlated with sudden bursts of short context completions which cause KV cache churn and small-batch tails. We suspect the K V metadata was being evicted too aggressively — transcription misread as "K V cash" in log labels.
[01:31] Carlos Vega: we ran a tail-sample, saw that some requests were getting queued for 400-500ms before being coalesced into a batch. That queuing delay is causing the p99 blowups, even though average token latency stays low.
[01:43] Priya Singh: question — how much of this is queue depth vs concurrency? If we cap concurrency at 160 do we avoid the p99 but lose throughput?
[01:50] Ravi Patel: good question. In our microbench, capping concurrency to 160 flattened the p99 to ~220ms but throughput dropped ~12%. With continuous batching we can reclaim some of that by increasing batch window slightly — e.g. batch_timeout 15ms and batch max 64 — but that increases avg latency. It's a tradeoff.
[02:10] Jenna Morris: what's the users' SLA on p95/p99? We need p95 < 150ms and p99 < 400ms ideally for interactive features.
[02:18] Maya Chen: right, customer stated p95 150ms p99 400ms in success criteria doc.
[02:22] Ravi Patel: so our proposal for the 4h steady-state run: start with concurrency target 220, queue depth 256, batch_timeout 12ms, max_batch 64. We'll monitor p95/p99 and have automatic rollback to concurrency 160 if p99 exceeds 420ms for more than 2 minutes. That gives us a path to measure cost & latency tradeoffs.
[02:44] Carlos Vega: curious, what about prefix caching? For our chat flows there is a frequent reuse of earlier tokens, so prefix or KV savings could reduce compute load.
[02:51] Ravi Patel: yes, prefix caching (we call it prefix KV caching in the playbook) is turned on for the conversational route; the pilot had cache hit ~18% — if we can push that to 30% by pinning embeddings or session affinity, that buys throughput back. We can share playbook steps for affinity headers.
[03:08] Tom Reyes: affinity headers meaning sticky session routing to the same GPU to keep KV warm?
[03:12] Ravi Patel: exactly, either cookie or session-id header that Redwood router uses. Note this has tradeoffs for horizontal spreading.
[03:19] Priya Singh: SRE question — what happens on sudden autoscale events, do we lose cache and spike latency?
[03:24] Ravi Patel: autoscale can affect KV warm state. Our fallback is cold-start mitigation: shorter cold-path batch sizes and immediate priority ramping for in-flight requests. In pilot we configured a warming backoff so newly provisioned nodes are drained into a slow ramp to avoid p99 spikes. That said, if you anticipate steady traffic ramps, reserved capacity is easier.
[03:44] Jenna Morris: we are evaluating reserved vs hosted — security and compliance may push reserved. We'll still want these tuning notes though.
[03:50] Maya Chen: quick note on cost controls — we enabled capped burst capacity of 30% to limit runaway spend during unexpected surge. That interacts with queueing because if burst is exhausted we'll hit queuing sooner.
[04:03] Carlos Vega: log question — what telemetry should we send? We have prometheus, jaeger and custom request logs.
[04:09] Ravi Patel: please attach request-level latency, batch sizes, batch_wait_time, queue_depth, model_variant, and KV_cache_hit. Also a small sample of raw tokens around p99 events helps. We'll give a template.
[04:21] Speaker 2 (Lena Ortiz): I'll drop links for the template on the notes channel after the call.
[04:27] [05:00] -- mid-call deep dive slides shared by Ravi (link: drive/redwood/pilot-playbook/aperture-june)
